title: When Israeli Rivals Agree: The Munitions Story Both Sides of Haaretz Believed
subtitle: Left-liberal Haaretz and centre-right Jerusalem Post both accepted the Washington Post's munitions account as credible — despite their divergence on almost everything else.
body_md:
The Washington Post reported on August 6 that US Patriot interceptor stocks had fallen by approximately 65 percent from pre-conflict levels since February, that more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and over 1,000 THAAD missiles had been fired at Iran in the conflict's first month, and that ATACMs — the short-range missile system Ukraine also depends on — were depleted to the point where there were "basically none left." [Jerusalem Post](https://www.jpost.com/international/article-904714) Trump responded on Truth Social that the United States had "massive amounts" of munitions and that "'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down" with "Long term jail sentences" to follow. [Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/08/06/world/trump-munitions-shortage/)

Haaretz, Israel's left-liberal daily, reported: "Report: Trump, Hegseth clash over missile shortage that could limit Iran strikes." Jerusalem Post, centre-right and broadly aligned with the Israeli security establishment, reported: "US President Donald Trump did not know about the extreme munitions shortage that is threatening to limit US military options in Iran." Both outlets treated the Washington Post account as credible. Neither led with Trump's denial. [Haaretz](https://www.haaretz.com/us-news/2026-08-06/ty-article/report-trump-hegseth-clash-over-missile-shortage-that-could-limit-iran-strikes/0000019f-d616-dabd-abdf-ff56d47e0000) This is the paradox the corpus surfaces: two Israeli outlets that diverge on virtually every political question converge completely on this one, reflecting a shared national-security interest that overrides editorial coloring. When Patriot interceptors are depleted, Israeli press politics yields to Israeli defense requirements.

Ten country groupings covered the story, converging around a shared military-readiness frame — but diverging meaningfully on emphasis. LaBSE mean similarity for the France bucket was 0.708, the lowest in the corpus, driven by a question-led structure: French outlets asked whether the US was actually running short of missiles rather than leading with Trump's rebuttal. BFM TV positioned CNN and the Washington Post as substantive claims requiring verification; France Info noted the shortages "affect Trump's strategy vis-à-vis Iran" without attribution to one side. [BFM TV](https://www.bfmtv.com/economie/entreprises/defense/les-etats-unis-commencent-ils-a-manquer-de-missiles-donald-trump-se-met-en-colere-nie-tout-et-fustige-les-medias-accuses-de-propager-des-affirmations-traitresses_AD-202608060213.html)

Japan Times was alone in citing the Pentagon's $67 billion emergency funding request to Congress — including $18.2 billion designated for replacing Patriot interceptors, Navy Tomahawks, and THAAD systems. That number provides a government-internal accounting of the shortage that Trump's denial cannot unsay. [Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/08/06/world/trump-munitions-shortage/) The Independent reported the Camp David confrontation: Trump confronted Defense Secretary Hegseth over the shortage, and Hegseth blamed his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, for failing to keep the president informed. [The Independent](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-hegseth-iran-war-weapons-shortage-b3028334.html)

Kyiv Post made the Ukraine spillover explicit: depleted ATACMs and frozen Patriot transfers to Ukraine are direct consequences of US-Iran conflict consumption. [Kyiv Post](https://www.kyivpost.com/post/81814) Jerusalem Post separately reported the ATACMs figure — citing Reuters data, an attribution exclusive to Israeli press — and noted that between February and July the US used "around 65% of its Patriot interceptors, leaving the country unwilling to supply Ukraine with the much needed defense system." Two countries named as the concrete third-party casualty of a bilateral US-Iran conflict: Ukraine losing weapons it was promised, while Israel tracked whether its primary air-defense supplier had the capacity to restock.

China and Russia are absent from this corpus. Both countries have obvious strategic interests in publicizing US military-capacity constraints — Russia directly, given its weapons and diplomatic alignment with Iran; China indirectly, given the implications for US credibility in any Taiwan scenario. Their absence from a cluster documenting the most detailed publicly reported US munitions inventory since the conflict began is not easily explained on editorial-interest grounds alone.

The jail-threat frame gave the story a second register alongside the military-readiness one. Across all 10 countries, Trump's warning that leakers face prosecution circulated alongside the depletion numbers. The two elements — "we have massive amounts" and "leakers will be jailed" — are logically in tension; only a shortage worth hiding requires jailing those who describe it.
